paragraphs: Rates fell on fear, not on data. The 10-year Treasury yield dropped about 19bp on Thu Oct 22 to ~4.95%, the biggest one-day fall since August 2025 and the first close under 5% since Sept 23, as money moved into bonds during that day's tech selloff. It ended Friday near 4.99%, down ~11bp on the week (third weekly decline) and below the ~5.10% at the Oct 18 pull. The Fed is in its blackout ahead of the Oct 27-28 FOMC. Odds of an October hike fell from ~15% to roughly 5-10%; a December hike is still priced at ~71%. The data didn't argue for a dovish turn. Jobless claims hit a three-month low (194K), Michigan's year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7%, and the October flash PMI showed output prices rising at the fastest pace since August 2022. Housing is weak: the NAHB index hit 29 (lowest since 2012) and September starts fell 5.9%.

Equities: the chip losing streak ended Monday, but the AI trade broke down again Thursday. Meta fell ~7% after raising capex guidance to $135-145B, Lam Research ~9% on light guidance and Tesla ~3% after a 43% drop in Q3 net income. The SOX fell 6%+, the Nasdaq 2.6% and the S&P 500 1.21% (worst day since July), while the Dow was flat and the Russell 2000 rose. Friday the selling broadened: the Dow fell 1.23%. On the week the S&P 500 was -0.47% and the Nasdaq -0.71% (second straight weekly loss for both); the Dow was +0.41% and the Russell 2000 +2.0%, a rotation out of crowded AI names. The VIX closed at 19.45, below the Oct 16 intraday high of 22.31.

Credit and oil kept tightening the screws. HY spreads widened 13bp to 3.40% on Oct 22 (FRED), concentrated in AI-linked debt: Oracle 5-year CDS reached a record ~315bp on Oct 19, and long-dated Oracle, CoreWeave and Nvidia bonds trade well below par. Brent settled at $116.72 on Fri Oct 23 (six-month high, third weekly gain) and WTI at $103.27, after Houthi strikes on Saudi targets (including a claimed fire at Aramco's Yanbu facility) and Iranian claims of seven tankers hit in Hormuz, of which monitors confirmed two. Gold fell to ~$4,008.

Data note: FRED's WTI series is again out of line with reported settles. It shows $110.01 on Oct 19 and $107.89 on Oct 20, while reported settles were $103.66 and $101.79. The narrative above uses reported prices. Several CNBC and Bloomberg figures (Oracle/CoreWeave CDS, the PMI) were confirmed from search summaries because the pages blocked access; FRED's Oct 23 credit and yield values had not posted on 10/24/26.

Rates and the Fed whipsawed on data rather than trending. The 10-year Treasury yield is lower than at the Oct 1 pull (5.10% on Oct 15 vs. ~5.2-5.3% around the end of September), but the path was not smooth. September payrolls (released Oct 2) rose just 29,000 vs. ~84,000 expected, with unemployment up to 4.2% and 60,000 of downward revisions, which pulled October-hike odds down to roughly 1 in 5. Then the hotter-than-expected September CPI on Oct 14 (headline 3.7% y/y vs. 3.6% expected; core 2.6% vs. 2.5%, driven largely by a 9.1% jump in gasoline) briefly sent the 10-year to ~5.28% intraday and CME odds of an Oct 27-28 hike to ~54%. Yields fell back on Oct 15 as investors rotated out of tech into bonds, and on Oct 16 Fed Chair Warsh, speaking in Bangkok, declined to signal October ('I don't prejudge meetings'), cutting hike odds to ~15%. Fed funds are unchanged at 3.75%-4.00%, and futures still price roughly one more hike by December.

Equities set records and then rolled over in tech. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at records on Oct 6 (7,818.93 and 27,599.79). Since then chips have fallen eight straight sessions, the longest streak since 2008, and the Nasdaq lost 4.5% in the week to Oct 16, its worst week since late June. Friday alone took the Nasdaq down 2.15%, the S&P 500 down 1.09% and the Russell 2000 down 1.66%, while the VIX touched 22.31 intraday. Coverage ties the selloff to a repricing of the AI capex cycle, unwinding of crowded AI positions and AI-debt stress. The Dow held up (+0.67% on the week), helped by rotation into health care, financials and energy.

Credit and oil are the new pressure points. The ICE BofA high-yield OAS has widened further, to 3.23% (about +53bp over the month), with IG at 0.84%, and the stress is concentrated in AI-linked debt. CoreWeave's 5-year CDS hit distress levels (reported near ~1,195bp) on Oct 15, and Goldman flagged a 25bp widening in HY AI-debt spreads over Oct 13-14. Oil reignited on Oct 16: Brent touched $110 for the first time since May and WTI settled at $101.41 (+3.5%) as Iran escalated attacks on Hormuz shipping, at least nine vessels since Oct 11, which is why energy names dominated Friday's gainers. The dollar index is up ~3.5% over the month.

Data note: FRED's WTI series (DCOILWTICO) again looks unreliable. It shows $101.91 on Oct 14, while Reuters-sourced reporting had WTI settling ~$94.14 on Oct 13 and trading ~$94-95 through Oct 14-15. WTI only reached ~$101 at Friday's Oct 16 settle. The narrative above uses independently reported prices, not FRED's levels.

newly_flagged.narrative: UPDATE (10/24/26): This flag now reflects Fri Oct 23, when the Dow fell 1.23% (-653 points) to 52,215.16 after holding up all week (flat on Thu Oct 22 even as the Nasdaq fell 2.6%). Friday's selling spread beyond the AI/tech names that drove Thursday into the broader market, with oil-sensitive groups such as airlines hit as Brent settled at $116.72 (+3.1%, a six-month high) on Houthi strikes on Saudi targets and Iranian claims of tanker hits in Hormuz. Even after Friday the Dow finished the week +0.41%, the only major index up, so this is a one-day oil/risk-off hit on a week of rotation into the Dow's non-tech names, not a rate shock like the September readings below. Prior framing: The Dow's -1.03% figure on 09/23/26 spans two real sessions compressed into one by the Sept 22 data gap described in the synthesis above. Tuesday Sept 22 the Dow slipped a modest 0.3% while the Nasdaq set a second straight record close - Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin struck a hawkish note ('supply shocks aren't proving short-lived'). Wednesday Sept 23 did the rest of the damage (-0.7%) as the 10-year Treasury yield jumped to roughly 5.11%-5.14% (highest since July 2007) after Fed Governor Michael Barr said 'further policy adjustments are likely to be needed,' and a hotter-than-expected S&P Global composite PMI (58.4 vs. 55.3 forecast) reinforced inflation concerns, pushing October-hike odds to ~66-74%. Same rate/inflation mechanism as the Sept 16 FOMC-day flag below, not a new independent driver. This flag now trips on the day-move threshold rather than the 5-day one, because the FOMC's Sept 16 hike hit in a single session: the Fed hiked 25bp as anticipated, and the Dow fell 631pts (-1.21%) to 51,461.90 on the day — banks led the damage (KBE -2.6%, worst day since February) on fears the hiking cycle continues into 2027. Broad-market and cyclical names have lagged over the past week as rising Treasury yields and oil prices weigh on rate-sensitive and industrial stocks more than mega-cap tech. A hot core CPI print (+0.3% m/m vs +0.2% forecast) raised the odds of a Fed hike at the Sept 15-16 FOMC meeting from ~70% to ~90%, and Iran's attacks on commercial/naval vessels in the Middle East have pushed oil higher, adding an inflation and cost headwind for industrials and consumer names that make up a larger share of the Dow than the Nasdaq.

newly_flagged.narrative: UPDATE (10/24/26): This flag now reflects Thu Oct 22, when the 10-year fell about 17bp on FRED's daily series (5.13% to 4.96%; Investrade's close is 4.953%, -19.3bp), the biggest one-day drop since August 2025 and the first close below 5% since Sept 23. The driver was a flight into bonds during that day's AI/tech selloff (Meta -7% on higher capex guidance, Lam Research -9%, the SOX -6%), not a data surprise: jobless claims that morning were a low 194K. The 5-year fell ~20bp and the 30-year ~15bp. October-hike odds fell to ~10.5%, and Bloomberg data put them near 5% on Oct 23 (from ~15% earlier in the week), with a December hike still priced at ~71%. Yields rose back to ~4.99% on Fri Oct 23 after an S&P Global flash PMI showed output prices rising at the fastest pace since August 2022. The 10-year was down ~11bp on the week, its third straight weekly decline. The Fed is in its pre-meeting blackout ahead of the Oct 27-28 FOMC. Prior framing: The FOMC met and hiked — 25bp to 3.75%-4%, a 12-0 vote, the first hike since 2023 — rather than the cut markets had been pricing earlier in the year. The 10-year yield broke through 5% on the decision (5.02% intraday) as Chair Warsh's press conference reinforced that inflation is still the Fed's binding constraint; the dot plot signals at least one more hike is possible before year-end. This confirms rather than reverses the move already described below. The 10-year Treasury yield's 12bp jump is the mechanical center of this week's story: a hotter-than-expected core CPI print (+0.3% m/m) pushed the market-implied odds of a Fed rate hike at the Sept 15-16 FOMC from ~70% to ~90%, and a global bond selloff (fiscal deficit concerns, heavy Treasury issuance) is compounding the move. Yields are now at their highest level since 2023, approaching the highest since 2007.

Semiconductors led the decline (SOXX headed for a ninth straight loss, 57 of 60 names in a chip basket down; software lost roughly $130B in market value, with Palantir -7% and Twilio -10%), compounded by renewed AI-financing worries (CoreWeave -12% on its debt-heavy balance sheet) and an oil spike - Brent touched $110 for the first time since May and WTI settled at $101.41 (+3.5%) as Iran escalated attacks on Hormuz shipping. Energy names were the session's big winners, which is why this dashboard's top-gainers list is almost all E&Ps and midstream. One partial offset: Fed Chair Warsh, speaking at an IMF event in Bangkok, declined to signal an October hike ('I don't prejudge meetings'), and CME odds of an Oct 27-28 hike fell to ~15% from ~28% before he spoke (they had jumped to ~54% after Wednesday's hot September CPI). The VIX jumped more than four points, briefly touching 22.31, its highest intraday level since June 11. For context, the index had closed at a record 7,818.93 on Oct 6. Prior framing: S&P 500 rose 1.49% on Monday, Sept 21 to 7,764.70 - its strongest session in weeks - as Treasury 10-year yields fell back under 5% (traders trimmed bets on a second 2026 Fed hike) and WTI crude eased from the prior week's highs, reversing two of the exact headwinds that drove the Sept 16 FOMC-day selloff described in the synthesis above. Chip and crypto strength broadened the move: the semiconductor rally sparked Sept 18 when Meta's new Muse AI agent hit the top of Apple's App Store (read by traders as bullish for CPU-side AI-inference demand, lifting Arm +13%/Intel +12%/AMD +9% that day) carried through the weekend, with AMD crossing a $1T market cap on Monday for the first time on its 5-day rally; bitcoin's surge past $85,000 the same day lifted Coinbase, Robinhood, and crypto-miner stocks.

The week's path: a hot September CPI on Wed Oct 14 (headline 3.7% y/y vs 3.6% expected, core 2.6% vs 2.5%; the 10-year yield rose to ~5.28% intraday) sent the Nasdaq and Russell 2000 down ~2% that day; Thursday Oct 15 the Nasdaq was flat (+0.08%) as investors rotated out of chips into other sectors and bonds (the 10-year fell back to 5.10%); and Friday's -2.15% chip/software rout finished the week. Prior framing: The 5-session window has rolled forward and now includes the Sept 22-23 pullback described in the DOW/RUSSELL2000 day-move flags above: Nasdaq set a second straight record close Tuesday Sept 22 (+0.4%) before falling roughly 1.1% Wednesday Sept 23 as the 10-year Treasury yield spiked to ~5.11% (highest since 2007) on hawkish Fed commentary and a hot PMI print. There is no genuinely new story here beyond what's already below - this reads as last week's rally holding up under a fresh bout of rate-driven selling, not being extended by a new catalyst. Nasdaq's 5-day change (Sept 15-21) turned solidly positive (+3.57%) even though the window contains the Sept 16 FOMC-hike selloff (Nasdaq -0.01% that day per the index data) - the index round-tripped and then broke higher on the Meta-Muse-triggered chip rally that began Sept 18 (Arm +13%, Intel +12%, AMD +9%) and continued through Monday Sept 21's broad rally (falling yields/oil, bitcoin above $85,000, AMD crossing a $1T market cap), which more than offset the FOMC-day losses within the same 5-day window.

The FOMC's Sept 16 hike (to 3.75%-4%, first since 2023) is the realization of the rate risk this flag was already tracking, and small-caps' higher rate sensitivity means they remain the most exposed index to it as the 10-year sits above 5%. Small caps are more rate-sensitive than large caps (higher average leverage, more floating-rate debt), so the run-up in the 10yr yield toward 5% on hot inflation data and hawkish Fed signaling has hit the Russell 2000 harder than large-cap indices over the past week. The same Middle East-driven oil spike also raises input costs disproportionately for smaller, less diversified companies.

material_events.narrative: UPDATE (10/24/26): This flag now reflects Thu Oct 22, when the 10-year fell about 17bp on FRED's daily series (5.13% to 4.96%; Investrade's close is 4.953%, -19.3bp), the biggest one-day drop since August 2025 and the first close below 5% since Sept 23. The driver was a flight into bonds during that day's AI/tech selloff (Meta -7% on higher capex guidance, Lam Research -9%, the SOX -6%), not a data surprise: jobless claims that morning were a low 194K. The 5-year fell ~20bp and the 30-year ~15bp. October-hike odds fell to ~10.5%, and Bloomberg data put them near 5% on Oct 23 (from ~15% earlier in the week), with a December hike still priced at ~71%. Yields rose back to ~4.99% on Fri Oct 23 after an S&P Global flash PMI showed output prices rising at the fastest pace since August 2022. The 10-year was down ~11bp on the week, its third straight weekly decline. The Fed is in its pre-meeting blackout ahead of the Oct 27-28 FOMC. Prior framing: The FOMC met and hiked — 25bp to 3.75%-4%, a 12-0 vote, the first hike since 2023 — rather than the cut markets had been pricing earlier in the year. The 10-year yield broke through 5% on the decision (5.02% intraday) as Chair Warsh's press conference reinforced that inflation is still the Fed's binding constraint; the dot plot signals at least one more hike is possible before year-end. This confirms rather than reverses the move already described below. The 10-year Treasury yield's 12bp jump is the mechanical center of this week's story: a hotter-than-expected core CPI print (+0.3% m/m) pushed the market-implied odds of a Fed rate hike at the Sept 15-16 FOMC from ~70% to ~90%, and a global bond selloff (fiscal deficit concerns, heavy Treasury issuance) is compounding the move. Yields are now at their highest level since 2023, approaching the highest since 2007.
